stem: A client stopped lisinopril because of a persistent ACE-inhibitor cough and is starting losartan. Which teaching about cough is most accurate?

options.A: A previous ACE-inhibitor cough makes losartan contraindicated even when there was no angioedema or hypersensitivity.
options.B: Losartan is expected to cause cough at approximately the same frequency as lisinopril in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough.
options.C: Losartan prevents medication-related cough completely, so any cough after the switch must have a nonmedication cause.
options.D: Cough can still occur with losartan, but in controlled trials of patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough it occurred substantially less often with losartan than with lisinopril.

rationale: The current DailyMed/FDA losartan label reports two randomized controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough. Cough occurred in 17% with losartan versus 69% with lisinopril in one trial and 29% versus 62% in the other; the label also notes postmarketing cases of cough with losartan, including positive rechallenges. Therefore D is correct: losartan can still be associated with cough, but cough was much less frequent than with lisinopril in these trials. A is incorrect because prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a listed contraindication to losartan, B contradicts the trial data, and C falsely treats cough risk as zero.
educational_objective: Teach clients switched from an ACE inhibitor to losartan that cough is less common with losartan than with lisinopril in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, but cough can still occur and should not automatically be dismissed.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
source_document_title: Losartan Potassium Tablets, for oral use
source_version_date: Updated January 13, 2026; prescribing information revised January 2026
source_locator: Adverse Reactions §6.1 > Cough: two controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough; Study 1 cough 17% losartan vs 69% lisinopril, Study 2 29% vs 62%; postmarketing cough including positive rechallenges reported. Contraindications §4 lists hypersensitivity and aliskiren coadministration in diabetes, not prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone.
source_claim_supported: In patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, losartan was associated with substantially less cough than lisinopril in controlled trials, although cough can still occur and prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a losartan contraindication.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify adverse medication effects, evaluate medication response, reconcile medication changes, and provide accurate client teaching about expected and reportable effects.

source_original.stem: A client stopped lisinopril because of a persistent ACE-inhibitor cough and is starting losartan. Which teaching about cough is most accurate?

options.A: A previous ACE-inhibitor cough makes losartan contraindicated even when there was no angioedema.
options.B: Losartan is expected to cause cough at approximately the same frequency as lisinopril in this situation.
options.C: Losartan prevents cough completely, so any cough after the switch must have a nonmedication cause.
options.D: Cough can still occur, but it was less frequent with losartan than lisinopril in trials of patients who previously had ACE-inhibitor cough.

source_original.rationale: DailyMed losartan labeling reports controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough in which cough occurred less frequently with losartan than with lisinopril. A prior cough alone is not equivalent to a contraindication to an ARB.
source_original.source_detail: Adverse Reactions — Cough: controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough compare losartan with lisinopril. DailyMed version 25; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring, reconciliation and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the switch-from-ACE-inhibitor construct and key D, added the source-supported point that cough remains possible with losartan, clarified that prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a losartan contraindication, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests direct label-based comparative adverse-effect teaching.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current DailyMed/FDA losartan label; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: DailyMed §6.1 Adverse Reactions > Cough, Table 1; §4 Contraindications
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately states the comparative cough findings and avoids claiming zero cough risk or a contraindication based only on prior ACE-inhibitor cough.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a listed losartan contraindication.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because controlled trials showed cough far less often with losartan than lisinopril.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because postmarketing cough with losartan has been reported and the risk is not zero.
distractor_audit.D: Correct and directly supported by the label's controlled-trial and postmarketing data.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D preserves both parts of the evidence: cough can still occur, but it was substantially less frequent with losartan than lisinopril in the relevant trial population.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address the same client-teaching issue; no unrelated pharmacology fact identifies the key.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — adverse-effect recognition and client teaching after medication change.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the January 2026 DailyMed label, cough trial data, postmarketing statement, contraindications, all four options, rationale, objective, difficulty, ambiguity, cueing, and NCSBN mapping. D remained uniquely correct.
